ep-meca-025.question: In a patient with overt ventricular pre-excitation (clear delta wave, Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome), what would you expect of the HV interval in sinus rhythm?
options: HV prolonged beyond 70 ms
Normal HV, between 35 and 55 ms
Short or even negative HV
HV unmeasurable, His never recorded
commentaires: Incorrect: a prolonged HV indicates His-Purkinje disease, unrelated to pre-excitation.
Incorrect: a normal HV is only possible if pre-excitation is minimal; with an obvious delta wave, it is shortened.
Correct: the accessory pathway activates the ventricle before or shortly after the His bundle; the HV is short, or even negative if pre-excitation is marked.
Incorrect: the His potential can still be recorded (with limited precision) and is unmasked if the accessory pathway blocks.
ep-meca-025.explication: With pre-excitation, part of the ventricle is activated early via the accessory pathway, which bypasses the AV node. The onset of ventricular activation (delta wave) therefore occurs before or shortly after the His potential: the HV is shortened, or even negative if pre-excitation is marked. This has nothing to do with His-Purkinje disease; His conduction remains measurable (with limited precision) and may be unmasked if the accessory pathway blocks. A normal HV is possible if pre-excitation is minimal, for example with a left lateral pathway far from the sinus node.

ep-meca-026.question: A patient undergoes an EP study for the conduction disturbance recorded on this tracing. On the His electrogram, every atrial deflection is followed by a His potential with a constant AH, but every other His potential is not followed by a ventricular electrogram. Where is the block?
options: Nodal (supra-Hisian)
Infra-Hisian
Intra-atrial
Undetermined without an atropine test
commentaires: Incorrect: nodal block would produce A without H; here, every A is followed by an H.
Correct: A followed by H, but H not followed by V, indicates block in the His-Purkinje system, which carries a poor prognosis and is an indication for pacing.
Incorrect: every atrial deflection is recorded and conducted to the His bundle; the block is not atrial.
Incorrect: atropine helps when only the surface ECG is available; here, the His electrogram localises the block directly.
ep-meca-026.explication: The tracing shows 2:1 AV block with wide QRS complexes. The site of block is read directly from the His electrogram. If the A is not followed by an H, the block is nodal (supra-Hisian). If the A is followed by an H but the H is not followed by a V, the block is infra-Hisian, in the His-Purkinje system. Here, the constant AH and the "orphan" H potentials indicate infra-Hisian block, which carries a poor prognosis and is a definite indication for pacing. The wide QRS of the conducted complexes is itself a clue to distal disease. An atropine challenge is useful when only the surface ECG is available; here, the intracardiac recording is sufficient.
ep-meca-026.aRetenir: A followed by H but H without V = infra-Hisian block, an indication for pacing.
ep-meca-026.legende: Rhythm strip recorded before the EP study

ep-meca-027.question: Two distinct His potentials (H and H') separated by an isoelectric interval are recorded on the His catheter, with some P waves blocked between H and H'. What is this?
options: Dual AV nodal physiology with an AH jump
A fasciculoventricular accessory pathway
A right bundle potential following the His
Intra-Hisian block (split His potential)
commentaires: Incorrect: dual AV nodal physiology manifests as a jump in the AH interval, not as two His potentials.
Incorrect: a fasciculoventricular pathway produces a short, fixed HV, without splitting of the His potential.
Incorrect: a right bundle potential follows the His by a few tens of ms, but P waves are never seen to block between the two.
Correct: separate H (proximal His) and H' (distal His) potentials, with P waves blocked between them, indicate intra-Hisian block, which may occur with narrow QRS complexes.
ep-meca-027.explication: A split His potential reflects conduction delay within the His bundle itself: H corresponds to the proximal portion and H' to the distal portion. If impulses block between H and H', this is intra-Hisian block, often associated with narrow QRS complexes because conduction below the block is normal. This is an important pitfall: high-grade AV block with narrow QRS complexes is not always nodal. Dual AV nodal physiology manifests as a jump in the AH interval, not as two His potentials. A fasciculoventricular pathway produces a short, fixed HV. A right bundle potential, recorded more distally, follows the His without P waves ever blocking between the two.
ep-meca-027.aRetenir: A split His potential (H-H') indicates intra-Hisian conduction disease, which may occur even with narrow QRS complexes.

ep-meca-028.question: Give the approximate normal values of the intracardiac PA, AH and HV intervals measured in sinus rhythm.
ep-meca-028.reponseAttendue: PA ≈ 20–60 ms; AH ≈ 50–120 ms (varies with autonomic tone); HV ≈ 35–55 ms.
ep-meca-028.explication: The PA interval (P-wave onset or high RA activation → low atrial activation on the His catheter) reflects intra-atrial conduction. The AH interval reflects nodal conduction and varies widely with vagal and sympathetic tone; commonly accepted normal values range from about 50 to 120 ms (55 to 125 ms in Josephson's series). The HV is the most stable interval, normally 35 to 55 ms. Exact values vary slightly between laboratories. A long PR interval may therefore reflect prolongation of any of these segments, and only a His bundle recording can determine which.
ep-meca-028.aRetenir: PA 20–60, AH 50–120, HV 35–55 ms: the EP study breaks down the PR interval.

ep-meca-029.question: A 72-year-old man with bifascicular block (RBBB + LAFB) has unexplained syncope after non-invasive work-up. The EP study shows an HV of 78 ms. What is the recommended management?
options: 24-hour Holter ECG monitoring
Tilt testing before any decision
Pacemaker implantation
Implantable loop recorder before any decision
commentaires: Incorrect: a 24-hour Holter has too low a diagnostic yield and would delay a decision that is already justified.
Incorrect: tilt testing has no first-line role when the EP study shows a positive criterion.
Correct: unexplained syncope + bifascicular block + HV ≥ 70 ms = pacing (class I, ESC 2018 and 2021).
Incorrect: an implantable loop recorder is considered when the EP study is negative; here, it is positive.
ep-meca-029.explication: In patients with unexplained syncope and bifascicular block, the ESC 2018 (syncope) and 2021 (pacing) guidelines recommend pacing (class I) in the presence of an HV ≥ 70 ms, second- or third-degree His-Purkinje block during incremental atrial pacing, or an abnormal response to pharmacological challenge. An HV of 78 ms is therefore a positive criterion: the syncope is very probably due to paroxysmal AV block. A 24-hour Holter has too low a diagnostic yield, and an implantable loop recorder is considered rather when the EP study is negative. Tilt testing has no first-line role here.
ep-meca-029.aRetenir: Syncope + bifascicular block + HV ≥ 70 ms = pacemaker (class I).

ep-meca-030.question: True or false: in a patient with LBBB and unexplained syncope, an HV of 62 ms is sufficient to establish an indication for a pacemaker.
options: True
False
commentaires: Incorrect: the statement is false; the decision threshold is an HV ≥ 70 ms, and 62 ms is not an indication in itself.
Correct: an HV of 62 ms calls for completion of the EP study (incremental pacing, pharmacological challenge), followed by an implantable loop recorder if it remains negative.
ep-meca-030.explication: This is false. The threshold adopted by the ESC 2018 and 2021 guidelines is an HV ≥ 70 ms. An HV of 62 ms, which is mildly prolonged, is not in itself an indication. The EP study must then be completed: incremental atrial pacing looking for infra-Hisian block and, if necessary, pharmacological challenge with a class I antiarrhythmic drug (ajmaline, procainamide, etc.). If the EP study remains negative, the next step is an implantable loop recorder to document the event, as the sensitivity of the EP study for paroxysmal AV block is imperfect. The pitfall: confusing a "prolonged" HV (> 55 ms) with an HV that is "abnormal in the decision-making sense" (≥ 70 ms).
ep-meca-030.aRetenir: The HV decision threshold in syncope with bundle branch block is ≥ 70 ms.

ep-meca-031.question: In a patient with unexplained syncope and bifascicular block, which EP study findings establish an indication for a pacemaker (ESC 2021)? (multiple answers)
options: Baseline HV ≥ 70 ms
Baseline HV between 55 and 69 ms
Second- or third-degree His-Purkinje block during incremental atrial pacing
Abnormal response to pharmacological challenge (class I antiarrhythmic drug)
AV nodal Wenckebach (progressive AH prolongation) during atrial pacing at 150 bpm
commentaires: Correct: a baseline HV ≥ 70 ms is sufficient to establish an indication for pacing (class I).
Incorrect: an HV between 55 and 69 ms is prolonged but below the decision threshold; the EP study must be completed.
Correct: infra-Hisian block during incremental atrial pacing indicates insufficient conduction reserve.
Correct: high-grade block or marked HV prolongation with ajmaline or procainamide is a positive criterion.
Incorrect: AV nodal Wenckebach at 150 bpm is physiological; it reflects the protective role of the AV node.
ep-meca-031.explication: The three recognised positive criteria are: baseline HV ≥ 70 ms, second- or third-degree infra-Hisian block during incremental atrial pacing, and high-grade block or marked HV prolongation during pharmacological challenge (ajmaline, procainamide or disopyramide depending on the country). A single criterion is sufficient to indicate pacing (class I). A mildly prolonged HV (between 55 and 69 ms) is not a criterion in itself and requires further investigation. Conversely, Wenckebach in the AV node during rapid atrial pacing is physiological: it reflects the protective role of the AV node. The classic pitfall is to regard any block appearing during atrial pacing as abnormal, without establishing its level (AH or HV).
ep-meca-031.aRetenir: Positive criteria: HV ≥ 70 ms, infra-Hisian block during atrial pacing, abnormal pharmacological challenge.

ep-meca-032.question: An HV ≥ 100 ms in a patient with bundle branch block classically indicates:
options: A trivial prolongation with no prognostic value of its own
A high risk of progression to high-grade AV block
Evidence in favour of dual AV nodal physiology
An effect of vagal tone, reversible with atropine
commentaires: Incorrect: Scheinman showed that the risk of complete AV block rises with the HV, steeply above 100 ms.
Correct: an HV ≥ 100 ms indicates severe His-Purkinje disease with a high risk of high-grade AV block; pacing is usually recommended.
Incorrect: dual AV nodal physiology is a nodal phenomenon, assessed on the AH, not the HV.
Incorrect: the His-Purkinje system receives very little vagal innervation; atropine does not correct a prolonged HV.
ep-meca-032.explication: Scheinman's studies of patients with bundle branch block showed that the risk of progression to complete AV block rises as the HV lengthens, becoming particularly high above 100 ms. An HV ≥ 100 ms is therefore a marker of severe His-Purkinje disease, which usually leads to a decision to pace, even when the case is less clear-cut. Current guidelines have adopted a threshold of 70 ms in patients with syncope. As the His-Purkinje system is barely sensitive to vagal tone, this prolongation is not corrected by atropine. The HV bears no relation to dual AV nodal physiology, a nodal phenomenon assessed on the AH.
ep-meca-032.aRetenir: HV ≥ 100 ms = severe His-Purkinje disease, high risk of high-grade AV block.

ep-meca-033.question: Successive ECGs in a patient show RBBB and then LBBB (alternating bundle branch block). What is the recommended management?
options: Pacemaker straight away, without a prior EP study
EP study first, pacemaker if HV ≥ 70 ms
Implantable loop recorder to document AV block
Observation alone if he remains asymptomatic
commentaires: Correct: alternating bundle branch block indicates unstable bilateral disease; pacing is class I, whether or not symptoms are present.
Incorrect: an EP study would add nothing to the decision and must not delay it.
Incorrect: waiting to document AV block exposes the patient to imminent complete AV block.
Incorrect: the indication for pacing also applies to asymptomatic patients.
ep-meca-033.explication: Alternating bundle branch block (RBBB and LBBB recorded at different times) reflects bilateral, unstable conduction system disease, with a high risk of imminent complete AV block. The ESC 2021 guidelines recommend pacing (class I) in these patients, whether symptomatic or not. An EP study would add nothing to the decision and must not delay it, any more than waiting for documentation by an implantable loop recorder. This should not be confused with RBBB alternating between different fascicular blocks, or with rate-related functional aberration.
ep-meca-033.aRetenir: Alternating bundle branch block = pacing straight away (ESC 2021, class I).

ep-meca-034.question: During incremental atrial pacing at 130 bpm in a patient with bifascicular block, some atrial deflections are followed by a His potential but no ventricular electrogram. How should this finding be interpreted?
options: Physiological AV nodal Wenckebach, of no consequence
An artefact related to His catheter position
Dual AV nodal physiology unmasked by pacing
Infra-Hisian block, a criterion for pacing
commentaires: Incorrect: AV nodal Wenckebach would produce A without H; here, the H is present and it is the V that is missing.
Incorrect: the His potential is clearly recorded; its failure to conduct to the ventricle is not an artefact.
Incorrect: dual AV nodal physiology manifests as a jump in the AH, not as an H without a V.
Correct: block below the His at a moderate rate indicates insufficient conduction reserve; it is a positive EP study criterion.
ep-meca-034.explication: During rapid atrial pacing it is normal for conduction to block, but at the level of the AV node (AH prolongation followed by an A without an H, i.e. AV nodal Wenckebach). Block appearing below the His (A-H conducted, H not followed by V) at a moderate rate indicates insufficient His-Purkinje conduction reserve. It is a positive EP study criterion for pacemaker implantation in a patient with syncope and bifascicular block. It must be confirmed that the block is not due to a premature beat or to a "long-short" sequence at the start of pacing, which can produce functional infra-Hisian block with no pathological significance.
ep-meca-034.aRetenir: Infra-Hisian block during incremental atrial pacing = abnormal criterion.

ep-meca-035.question: A frail 89-year-old woman with bifascicular block has recurrent unexplained syncope causing injury. What do the ESC 2021 guidelines suggest?
options: Empirical pacing is an option without an EP study (IIb)
EP study mandatory before any pacing (class I)
Implantable loop recorder first, pacing if AV block is documented
Pacing contraindicated without documented AV block (class III)
commentaires: Correct: in frail elderly patients at high risk of serious falls, the ESC 2021 guidelines allow empirical pacing without an EP study (IIb).
Incorrect: an EP study is not mandatory in this particular situation; waiting may expose the patient to serious injury.
Incorrect: this is the usual approach in other patients, but in this frail patient empirical pacing may be considered.
Incorrect: no such contraindication exists; the decision is individualised.
ep-meca-035.explication: In elderly, frail patients with bifascicular block and unexplained syncope, at high risk of recurrence or injury, the ESC 2021 guidelines allow empirical pacing to be considered without a prior EP study (class IIb). This is an individualised decision, weighing the risk of invasive investigation or of waiting for documentation by an implantable loop recorder against the risk of a serious fall. In most other patients, the approach remains an EP study followed, if negative, by an implantable loop recorder. Other causes of syncope, particularly reflex or orthostatic syncope, which are common at this age, must also be considered.
ep-meca-035.aRetenir: Frail elderly patient + bifascicular block + unexplained syncope: empirical pacing is an option (IIb).

ep-meca-036.question: How is the corrected sinus node recovery time (CSNRT) calculated?
options: SNRT minus the baseline sinus cycle length
SNRT divided by the baseline sinus cycle length
SNRT minus the PR interval
SNRT multiplied by the sinus rate
commentaires: Correct: CSNRT = SNRT − baseline sinus cycle length; abnormal if ≥ 525 ms.
Incorrect: the SNRT/baseline cycle length ratio exists, but it is not the CSNRT.
Incorrect: the PR interval plays no part in measuring sinus node recovery.
Incorrect: this calculation has no physiological meaning; the correction is made by subtracting the baseline cycle length.
ep-meca-036.explication: The SNRT (sinus node recovery time) is the interval between the last stimulus of a prolonged period of high atrial pacing (30 to 60 s) and the first spontaneous sinus P wave. As it depends on the baseline sinus rate, it is corrected by subtracting the spontaneous sinus cycle length: CSNRT = SNRT − baseline cycle length. A CSNRT ≥ 525 ms is considered abnormal by the ESC 2018 syncope guidelines. There is also an SNRT/baseline cycle length ratio, but this is not the CSNRT. Secondary pauses, occurring a few cycles after pacing stops, should also be sought.
ep-meca-036.aRetenir: CSNRT = SNRT − baseline sinus cycle length, abnormal if ≥ 525 ms.
